questions.q: A test gives **p = 0.03**. Which statement is correct?
options: If the null hypothesis were true, data at least this extreme would turn up about 3% of the time
There is a 97% probability that the effect is real
There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 3% probability that the result is due to chance
questions.why: A p-value is computed assuming H₀ is true; it measures how surprising the data are under H₀. It is not the probability that H₀ is true, nor that the effect is real; those depend on prior plausibility and power. "Due to chance" is a disguised version of the same mistake.

questions.q: A test returns "fail to reject H₀". What does that mean?
options: The null hypothesis has been proved true
The data were not surprising enough to rule out "no effect"; the effect may be zero or the test may have been too small to detect it
The alternative hypothesis has been proved false
The test was carried out incorrectly
questions.why: Not rejecting H₀ is a statement about weak evidence, not proof of no effect. A small or noisy test can easily miss a real effect. Check the confidence interval to see which effect sizes are still plausible.

questions.q: A coin lands heads 59 times in 100 tosses. Using the normal approximation, test H₀: p = 0.5 two-sided at α = 0.05.
options: z = 1.8, p ≈ 0.036, reject H₀
z = 9, p < 0.001, reject H₀
z = 1.8, p ≈ 0.072, do not reject H₀
z = 0.09, p ≈ 0.93, do not reject H₀
questions.why: Under H₀ the mean is 50 and the SD √(100 × 0.5 × 0.5) = 5, so z = 9 / 5 = 1.8. The two-sided p-value is 2 × 0.036 = 0.072, above 0.05 (the exact binomial test gives 0.089). Quoting 0.036 is the one-sided tail, a common way to overstate evidence; z = 9 forgets to divide by the SD.

questions.q: Which change **increases** the power of a test to detect a real effect of a given size?
options: Lowering α from 0.05 to 0.01
Increasing the sample size
Using a noisier metric
Switching from a one-sided to a two-sided test
questions.why: Power rises with larger samples, larger true effects, less noise and a less strict α. A stricter α (0.01) makes rejection harder and lowers power; a two-sided test splits α across both tails, which also lowers power in the direction of interest.

questions.q: An A/B test reports a lift of 1.0 point, 95% CI 0.19 to 1.81 points, p = 0.016. Which statement is correct?
options: The data are hard to explain with zero lift, and the plausible true lift ranges from about 0.2 to 1.8 points; finance should value both ends
The effect is large because the p-value is small
There is a 98.4% chance the new button is better
The true lift is exactly 1.0 point
questions.why: The small p-value says the data would be surprising if the buttons were equivalent, and the interval gives the range of lifts consistent with the data. A p-value is not the probability the effect is real, and it does not measure size: a tiny effect can have a tiny p-value with enough data.

questions.q: A company tests 1,000 ideas, of which 200 truly work. Each test uses α = 0.05 and has 80% power. What share of the ideas declared significant are actually duds?
questions.why: True positives = 80% of 200 = 160. False positives = 5% of 800 = 40. Share of winners that are false = 40 / 200 = 20%. 5% is α, the false-positive rate among useless ideas, not among significant results. 36% is the answer when only 100 of the ideas work, which shows the base rate drives it.

questions.q: A marketing campaign test is "not significant", with 95% CI for the lift of −1% to +6%. The CMO wants to cancel the campaign as useless. What is the flaw?
options: None; not significant means the effect is zero
The p-value must have been below 0.05
The test was inconclusive: the interval still includes a large benefit (up to +6%), so it could not tell; a bigger test is needed before concluding "no effect"
The interval shows the campaign is harmful
questions.why: Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. An interval from −1% to +6% is consistent with no effect, a small harm or a large gain. It does not show harm either, since most of it is above zero. The right move is to judge whether a larger test is worth it.

questions.q: In an interview: "Your two-sided A/B test gave p = 0.08. A colleague suggests switching to a one-sided test to get p = 0.04. Is that acceptable?"
options: Yes, one-sided tests are always valid
Yes, as long as the effect is in the hoped-for direction
No, because one-sided tests cannot be used for proportions
No; choosing the direction after seeing the data halves the p-value dishonestly and doubles the false-positive rate in that direction; the sidedness must be fixed in advance
questions.why: A one-sided test is legitimate only if you decided before seeing the data that the other direction does not matter. Switching after the fact is p-hacking. Checking that the effect went the hoped-for way is exactly what makes the switch dishonest.
